/world/2026/oct/28/spain-train-crash-hig.headline: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
/world/2026/oct/28/spain-train-crash-hig.excerpt: Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety. Officials said at least 68 people were killed on Wednesday morning after a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were believed to be carrying 544 passengers. Speaking to reporters, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, traced the collision back to a security system that had stopped working at about 8.30am local time. The computer malfunction brought an estimated six trains to a halt along a 63km stretch of track. Soon after, the central command in Madrid instructed one of the trains involved in the crash to resume service at normal speeds, sending it colliding into a train that was still sitting stationary on the tracks, said Puente. “It was the control centre – via its operators – that made the decision to resume operations, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he added. State-owned rail operator Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”. The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.headline: Israel election: what we know so far
/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.excerpt: With almost all votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government has lost its majority, but his main opponents, an alliance of Jewish Israeli parties unofficially led by Gadi Eisenkot, have also failed to gain an outright majority. Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 53 seats under the current vote share, but this could change further. The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 48 seats and the Palestinian parties on 19 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset. The remainder of votes to be counted come from absentee ballots, according to Israeli media. We can expect absentee ballots to be counted on Wednesday night, with final results by Thursday. The Palestinian Israeli parties have received a historically strong vote. The Joint List, a new ticket of several Arab-majority parties, triumphed with at least 12 seats, while Ra’am, the other Islamic party, won seven. The key question is whether the Eisenkot-led “Change” bloc (consisting of the rightwinger Naftali Bennett’s Together party, the centre-left Yair Golan’s Democrats and the rightwing Yisrael Beiteinu party) will partner with Palestinian Israeli parties or if they will resort to a new election, or even working with Netanyahu. Netanyahu took the stage at a post-election rally in Jerusalem just after 3am, telling his supporters that official results will show that “Likud is the largest party in Israel”.

/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.headline: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape
/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.excerpt: The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival. In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that. The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, which are projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored. The exit polls placed Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s governing coalition tied. Though the prime minister’s Likud party could still be the strongest single party, neither side has enough to get 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament for a majority. If confirmed by actual results, that would give Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, discretion over who he asks first to try to form a government. If one candidate cannot succeed in six weeks, the challenge is passed on to the next option. It could be an extremely long process, and all this time Netanyahu’s coalition would stay on in a caretaker role. Eisenkot could argue he has a chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority.
/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.trail: Exit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing

/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.headline: Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seats
/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.excerpt: Israel’s election appeared to have delivered no clear winner on Tuesday night after a historic turnout by voters for an election described by some as the most consequential in the country’s history, and marked by a record participation by Israeli Arab voters. Exit polls published on Tuesday evening suggested that the opposition bloc of parties led by the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, would win most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin, edging out Benjamin Netanyahu’s right and far-right coalition despite the prime minister’s Likud emerging as the largest party. The result is likely to set off weeks of jockeying over who can form a coalition government before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is called, but represents a sharp electoral rebuke to Netanyahu. After a day in which Israelis streamed to polling stations across the country, exit polls suggested Netanyahu’s ability to command the loyalty of a large core of Likud party voters remained undimmed despite his rejection by large numbers of Israelis. The predicted haul of up to 18 Knesset seats for Israeli Arab parties is likely to make them the kingmakers in what seem certain to be protracted talks to form a new government, with Netanyahu likely to fall short of the support required to form a new coalition. While Eisenkot could theoretically assemble a majority by forming a government with the Arab parties, he ruled that out before the election.

/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.headline: Legacy of 7 October looms large as a divided Israel goes to the polls in record numbers
/world/2026/oct/28/israel-election-exit-.excerpt: Election day in Israel began with a protest by some of the voters with most at stake. Bereaved families of those killed in the 7 October attacks held a minute of silence at 6.29am, the moment when Hamas launched its onslaught just over three years ago. They gathered in a Tel Aviv plaza that has become known as “hostages square” because it was the centre of demonstrations demanding the return of more than 200 captives from Gaza. Holding pictures of their loved ones, they stood in silence then called on voters to remember the losses and betrayals of that day when deciding on the next government. “Three years after the massacre, our loved ones will not be voting today. Go out and vote – remember them at the ballot box. This is what these elections are about,” the group said. They are not explicitly backing any political party, but one of their key demands is a state commission of inquiry into the attacks. Benjamin Netanyahu has resisted this and it has become a rallying point for the opposition parties trying to unseat him as prime minister. Netanyahu’s strongest challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, started the day by visiting communities attacked on 7 October. “If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here,” said the former military chief and leader of the Yashar party. Standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of “the worst government Israel has known”.

Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing. Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran. On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.

/world/2026/oct/28/european-union-canada.headline: EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence
/world/2026/oct/28/european-union-canada.excerpt: EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027. EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine, but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will call on the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, to contribute to Ukraine’s looming financial shortfall at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week. A similar request to the British prime minister will be made when he meets von der Leyen and the European Council president, António Costa, for a long-awaited EU-UK summit on 20 November in Brussels. It comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, prepares for his first budget next week, weighing numerous calls for more spending against the rising cost of government borrowing and a darkening economic outlook. Healey said earlier this month he was “working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine – military, diplomatic and economic”. Ukraine says it faces a €70bn (£58bn) funding shortfall in 2027 to pay for its defence and civilian needs. The EU and its member states are paying for 80% of Ukraine’s financial needs, according to the commission, which considers a “fair” EU share to be two-thirds, with the remaining third covered by other allies.

/world/2026/oct/28/european-union-canada.headline: EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ request
/world/2026/oct/28/european-union-canada.excerpt: The Trump administration pressured multiple countries to withdraw their sponsorship of a leading European conference on disinformation, with Canada, Lithuania and the EU’s diplomatic service subsequently agreeing to do so, the Guardian understands. The conference, #Disinfo2026, taking place on Wednesday and Thursday, is the annual meetup of Europe’s counter-disinformation community and has drawn hundreds of researchers, journalists, technologists and policymakers to a hotel in Vilnius, Lithuania. It is run by an independent Brussels non-profit, EU Disinfo Lab. Days before the conference, the logos of its main supporters – the Lithuanian ministry of foreign affairs, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry – were wiped off its website. Photos of the event shared with the Guardian also show white stickers affixed over the logos of these organisations printed on official conference materials, appearing to indicate they were struck from the program in haste. Three persons familiar with the matter, including European officials, confirmed that the US state department had been in touch with multiple governments over their support for the conference. Internal state department documents seen by the Guardian also show US officials thanking Lithuania for “taking US concerns seriously”.

/world/2026/oct/28/european-union-canada.excerpt: Mark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member. Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion. One day earlier, in the same debating chamber, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, issued the unprecedented invitation to Canada – an idea quickly derided by Donald Trump, who threatened Europe with “heavy tariffs” if it became a reality. But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions. So people are talking more about what an associate membership means instead of … this unique partnership and alliance for the future that EU-Canada relations should be about.” The German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesperson welcomed the initiative for a close partnership with Canada and said Germany was “open to discussing new models that reflect the special significance of the relationship”, but called for the associate membership label to be “reconsidered”.

/uk-news/2026/oct/28/knifeman-on-lner-tr.headline: ‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse
/uk-news/2026/oct/28/knifeman-on-lner-tr.excerpt: During lockdown, Charlotte and her ex-partner would spend evenings cooped up in their flat, listening to music, watching YouTube videos and chatting until the small hours. Those nights would be fuelled by alcohol and lines of cocaine. “I wanted to be loved, and when he told me he loved me like nobody ever would and nobody ever will, I drank the Kool-Aid,” Charlotte says. “I wanted to believe that. And there’s a point when you’re with somebody and you’re drinking, you’re doing coke, where you think you have this bond, you think it’s just you two in the world.” But that emotional high would be fleeting. “Without a doubt, without any exception, it would never end peacefully. My ex-partner would get so ridiculously paranoid once he was using cocaine. It was just crazy,” she says. Charlotte’s partner would accuse her of taking more than him, messaging men and hiding things from him. When she denied it, he would subject her to brutal physical assaults. “And then the next day it was all apologies and it’ll all be fine, it’ll all be different.” Data suggests it is a common scenario. /uk-news/2026/oct/28/knifeman-on-lner-tr.headline: Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s multibillion-pound cocaine habit
/uk-news/2026/oct/28/knifeman-on-lner-tr.excerpt: From pub toilets and private parties to football terraces and far-right marches, cocaine has become a familiar presence across modern Britain. Deaths linked to the drug have risen to record levels, while its supply supports a multibillion-pound criminal industry. But who is using the drug, and how has the picture changed? The figures do not necessarily show millions of new users, but highlight an established market in which some people take more cocaine, more often – and face greater harm as they grow older. *** A £9.8bn-a-year habit? In June this year the scientists at the Home Office published a new experimental estimate of cocaine consumption. Samples taken from sewage suggested that cocaine use rose by 26% between 2021 and 2025. They estimated that people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25: the equivalent of roughly 2.5bn lines, with an estimated street value of £9.8bn. Yet crime survey data suggests the number of people reporting cocaine use in the past year has remained flat or fallen slightly since the pandemic. One explanation is that a similar or smaller number of people are using the drug more frequently. Another is that the survey excludes people who are homeless or living in institutions, and some respondents may be reluctant to admit to illegal drug use. Dr Josh Torrance, a specialist in drug markets, says wastewater analysis can reveal use that surveys miss.

/uk-news/2026/oct/28/knifeman-on-lner-tr.headline: Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges
/uk-news/2026/oct/28/knifeman-on-lner-tr.excerpt: British police are recording a growing number of crimes linked to cocaine, including assaults, domestic abuse and dangerous driving, as figures show consumption has surged across England. A Guardian investigation has found police forces across Britain recorded a 10% rise in crime rates associated with the class A drug since 2019, while the Home Office estimates cocaine usage at sites across England has risen by 26% since 2021. Cocaine is a powerful and addictive stimulant that causes euphoria, overconfidence, restlessness and paranoia. Experts have warned its use can cause already fraught situations to escalate, potentially leading to violent incidents. The rise in consumption in recent years can be partly explained by historically low costs, while purity levels have remained high. Analysis of wastewater suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25. That’s equivalent to roughly 2.5bn lines of cocaine, at an estimated street value of almost £10bn. Police recorded at least 29,922 crimes mentioning the word cocaine in 2025 – equivalent to 63.4 for every 100,000 people. That was up from 57.7 cases for every 100,000 in 2019. Figures up to May this year suggest that number could increase again in 2026 to about 64 cases in every 100,000 people – a rise of more than 10% over seven years.

A separate Ukrainian strike in part of the north-eastern Kharkiv region held by Russia killed at least three people and gravely wounded another on Saturday, the Moscow-backed authorities said. Drones also rained down inside Russia. The country’s defence ministry said 616 of them had been shot down overnight across more than 20 regions of the country. During the day, drones hit Russia’s south-western Bryansk border region, killing at least three people, regional acting governor Yegor Kovalchuc said on Telegram. In Ukraine, authorities said that at least five people died in several Russian drone and missile strikes in the country’s east.

His legal team argued that publishing them would “highly likely lead him to commit suicide”. In written submissions to the court in London, the news outlets said the allegations involved more than 30 sources with first-hand accounts, as part of a “wide-ranging and rigorous investigation”. However, at the opening of a two-day trial, PPT’s legal team argued it was a “highly exceptional” case in which publishing was likely to lead to the death of the claimant. In a written submission to the court, the claimant’s legal team said that he suffered from “very severe mental health problems”. “It is important to understand that this drastic effect on the claimant is not from guilt of the wrongdoing alleged (which is denied) but because of shame arising from deep-rooted childhood trauma and the fear of ‘trial by media’,” it stated. Sara Mansoori KC, PPT’s lead barrister, said that he had first attempted to kill himself in May, when the Guardian and ITN contacted him to give him the chance to respond to the allegations. /uk-news/2026/oct/28/guardian-itn-duty-t.headline: Drumcree standoff shows Northern Ireland’s troubled past still threatens its peace
/uk-news/2026/oct/28/guardian-itn-duty-t.excerpt: Like a ghost from its troubled past, Drumcree has unexpectedly reappeared to remind people how far Northern Ireland has changed in 30 years but also how easily history can undermine the present, if imperfect, peace and stability. Three decades ago parts of Northern Ireland came to an almost annual standstill as Protestant Orange Order protesters blocked roads in support of members wanting to march down what they called its traditional route, the Garvaghy Road, on the Sunday before the annual 12 July parade. Because the Garvaghy Road is a main thoroughfare in a predominantly nationalist area, residents opposed the march. The standoff led to violence and murders at a time when Northern Ireland’s fragile peace process was in its infancy. In 1998, the newly formed Parades Commission was established to defuse tension around controversial marches and to regulate parades. The commission, which was opposed by the Orange Order and unionist political parties, banned the Drumcree parade and has done so every year since, until 2026. In August, the high court overturned a Parades Commission ruling preventing the march, saying the commission had erred in not following its own rules and procedures in its decision. That Parades Commission ruling has been described by the Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, as “incomprehensible and wrong”.

/uk-news/2026/oct/28/guardian-itn-duty-t.headline: Injunction blocking publication of ex-SAS soldier’s book on counter-terror op extended
/uk-news/2026/oct/28/guardian-itn-duty-t.excerpt: An injunction preventing a former member of the SAS from publishing a book about his role in a counter-terrorism operation has been extended after an application by the Ministry of Defence. The block on publication of the book in the UK will continue until the conclusion of a government legal action against the soldier, who is known only by the pseudonym Christian Craighead. Craighead received the Conspicuous Gallantry Cross – a medal one level down from the Victoria Cross – for his involvement in an incident after an al-Shabaab attack in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi in 2019 in which 21 people died. Craighead claims to have saved more than 700 people from a hotel complex in Nairobi after a group of armed militants launched an assault. The MoD claims that Craighead’s book contains an alleged breach of a confidentiality contract that he had freely signed on joining the UK’s special forces. An interim injunction was issued this month, with government barristers returning to the high court on Thursday to ask for it to be extended until the legal claim is resolved. Oliver Sanders KC, for the MoD, told the court in London the claim that Craighead had breached the contract was “straightforward and really unarguable”. The book has been published in the US but Sanders said that this was not relevant because “the only reason it is available overseas is through the defendant’s own wrongdoing”. Craighead did not appear in court and was not represented.

/media/2026/oct/28/allison-pearson-daily.headline: ‘Significant unease’ at the Telegraph over Reform using outlet for ‘spoiler’ tactics
/media/2026/oct/28/allison-pearson-daily.excerpt: The Telegraph and Reform UK are facing claims of undermining public interest journalism and eroding trust between reporters and politicians, after Nigel Farage’s party gave the newspaper stories first uncovered by other outlets. It is understood there is unease among editorial staff at the Telegraph about Reform’s repeated use of the outlet for “spoilers”: a media tactic designed to pre-empt a problematic story by placing it with a title seen as more sympathetic. The concern comes after the Telegraph published details of two unprecedented £36m donations to Reform from the crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne. It did so shortly after Farage and a party spokesperson had been approached for comment about the donations by the Sunday Times. “A fundamental part of political reporting – approaching for comment before publishing – just totally breaks down if this is what happens,” said the Sunday Times political editor, Ben Riley-Smith. “Bad for both sides: [It] will increase the chance of inaccuracies.” It follows similar instances in which Reform has attempted to use the Telegraph to neutralise potentially damaging stories. In April, the Guardian revealed that Farage had received a £5m gift from Harborne. When the Guardian went to Reform for comment, the party asked for more time to respond – and used the time to brief the Telegraph, which ran fawning interviews with Farage and Harborne.

/media/2026/oct/28/allison-pearson-daily.headline: Right turn on green: is the Telegraph changing its tune on the climate?
/media/2026/oct/28/allison-pearson-daily.excerpt: “Nobody can deny that the UK is getting warmer and high temperatures are becoming a clear threat to homes, nature and food security,” read the lengthy news report, which explored the devastating effect of British wildfires on families in recent years. The article’s conclusions, written after the wildfires in Suffolk last week, were no surprise given the UK’s changing climate. However, the fact that the piece appeared in the Telegraph, the rightwing title that has been a leading critic of green policies, did raise eyebrows among some readers. Praising the analysis, the independent MP Rosie Duffield noted it was from an outlet “hardly known for their raging lefty/net zero/climate change agenda”. Even more intriguing was the fact that the essay came after two other notable Telegraph climate pieces. The first was by the columnist Tim Stanley, who set off a debate on the right with an article headlined: “Climate change is real – and the right needs to get serious about it.” Then came a piece by the Telegraph’s respected world economy editor, Ambrose Evans-Pritchard, who has long argued that the costs of climate change could not be ignored. He accused Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, of choosing “an abominable political moment to flirt with climate nihilism”, citing her opposition to net zero targets and purge of candidates who back them. “There comes a point when you have to conclude that the Tories have gone Trumpian on the existential issue of our time,” he wrote.
